sections.section_title: Behçet’s Disease, Neuro-Behçet’s Disease, and SIADH: Core Concepts for This Case
sections.description: This section introduces the background knowledge necessary to understand the case: the clinical spectrum of Behçet’s disease, the forms of neurological involvement in neuro-Behçet’s disease, and the physiology and diagnostic framework of SIADH. It should focus specifically on concepts that directly inform the patient’s presentation and diagnostic reasoning.
subtopics: Overview of Behçet’s disease as a multisystem inflammatory vasculitic disorder
Typical mucocutaneous manifestations: oral aphthae, genital ulcers, folliculitis-like or papulopustular skin lesions
International diagnostic criteria for Behçet’s disease and how points are assigned
Epidemiology and timing of neurological involvement in Behçet’s disease
Clinical subtypes of neuro-Behçet’s disease: acute parenchymal/meningoencephalitic presentations versus other neurological patterns
How acute neuro-Behçet’s disease can present with headache, fever, vertigo, meningitic symptoms, behavioural change, or focal deficits
Why normal brain MRI does not exclude acute neuro-Behçet’s disease, especially early or non-parenchymal disease
ADH physiology and normal regulation of water balance
Definition and diagnostic criteria of SIADH in euvolemic hypo-osmolar hyponatraemia
Common causes of SIADH, with emphasis on CNS inflammation, malignancy, pulmonary disease, and medications
Potential inflammatory links between neuro-Behçet’s disease and SIADH, including the hypothesised role of IL-6

sections.description: This section reconstructs the patient’s early clinical picture and teaches learners how to synthesize scattered findings into a coherent problem representation. It should show how mucocutaneous symptoms, constitutional features, neurological complaints, and hyponatraemia together created a complex but interpretable presentation.
subtopics: Chronology of presentation: fever, headache, malaise, anorexia, hiccups, arthralgia, and oral aphthae
Relevant past history and contextual factors: untreated type 2 diabetes, social history, exposure history, and family history
Physical examination findings and their diagnostic implications
Recognition of the mucocutaneous phenotype suggestive of Behçet’s disease
Assessment of mental status, focal neurological signs, meningeal signs, and volume status
Clinical significance of persistent hiccups in the setting of hyponatraemia and CNS disease
Interpretation of initial inflammatory markers and associated laboratory abnormalities
Understanding elevated creatine kinase in this context, including the possibility of rhabdomyolysis from hyponatraemia
Constructing an initial problem representation: febrile inflammatory syndrome with headache, aseptic CNS features, mucocutaneous lesions, and euvolemic hyponatraemia
Early priorities in stabilization and broad diagnostic triage

sections.section_title: Diagnostic Workup and Clinical Reasoning from Broad Differential to Definite Diagnosis
sections.description: This section explains how the clinicians moved stepwise from a nonspecific inflammatory-neurological presentation to the linked diagnoses of definite Behçet’s disease, acute neuro-Behçet’s disease, and SIADH. The focus should be on disciplined differential diagnosis, targeted interpretation of tests, and the logic of exclusion and pattern recognition.
subtopics: Initial differential diagnosis for fever, headache, and hyponatraemia: CNS infection, systemic inflammatory disease, malignancy, and other autoimmune conditions
Interpretation of serum sodium, serum osmolality, urine osmolality, urinary sodium, and ADH level in diagnosing SIADH
Excluding alternative endocrine causes of hyponatraemia: thyroid and adrenal insufficiency
Role of euvolemic examination and normal renal function in supporting SIADH
Evolution of neurological symptoms and rationale for lumbar puncture
CSF profile of aseptic meningitis: mild lymphocytic pleocytosis and elevated protein
Use and limitations of brain MRI in suspected acute neuro-Behçet’s disease
How infectious causes were excluded: bacterial, mycobacterial, HSV, VZV, and cryptococcal testing
Consideration and de-prioritisation of CNS malignancy based on imaging, cytology, and nonspecific sIL-2R elevation
Why neurosarcoidosis and other autoimmune diseases were considered but not supported
Appearance of genital ulcer as a pivotal diagnostic clue
Application of International Criteria for Behçet’s Disease to establish definite systemic Behçet’s disease
Role and limitations of HLA-B51 testing in diagnosis
Final diagnostic synthesis: concurrent systemic Behçet’s disease, acute neuro-Behçet’s disease presenting as aseptic meningitis, and SIADH likely related to CNS inflammation

sections.section_title: Management Decisions: Treating Inflammation, Neurological Disease, and Hyponatraemia
sections.description: This section examines the treatment strategy in the acute setting, including empiric therapies given before the diagnosis was clear, the eventual choice of colchicine monotherapy, and conservative management of SIADH. It should also compare this approach with standard treatment expectations for acute neuro-Behçet’s disease.
subtopics: Principles of empiric management when CNS infection remains possible
Rationale for starting cefepime and later empiric acyclovir
De-escalation of antimicrobials after microbiological exclusion of infection
Standard therapy for acute neuro-Behçet’s disease and the usual role of corticosteroids
When immunosuppressive agents are considered in neuro-Behçet’s disease
Mechanism of action of colchicine relevant to Behçet’s disease: neutrophil inhibition and cytokine suppression
Established role of colchicine in mucocutaneous Behçet’s disease
Why colchicine monotherapy in acute neuro-Behçet’s disease is unusual and clinically notable
Local treatment of oral, genital, and skin lesions
Conservative SIADH management: fluid restriction, sodium monitoring, and prevention of overly rapid correction
Indications for hypertonic saline or vasopressin antagonists and why they were unnecessary here
Clinical judgment in avoiding corticosteroids or other immunosuppressants in this patient

sections.section_title: Outcome, Pathophysiologic Interpretation, and Clinical Lessons
sections.description: This section consolidates what happened after treatment, interprets the relationship among Behçet’s disease, neuro-Behçet’s disease, and SIADH, and distills the main teaching points for practice. It should help learners understand both the limits and the significance of the case.
subtopics: Clinical course after colchicine initiation: resolution of fever, appetite loss, vertigo, malaise, hiccups, and mucocutaneous lesions
Normalization of serum sodium and reduction in ADH level over time
Recovery of creatine kinase and other laboratory abnormalities
Hospital discharge, rehabilitation needs, and long-term follow-up
Four-year remission on continued colchicine without recurrence of neurological or Behçet’s symptoms
Possible pathophysiologic model linking CNS inflammation to SIADH in acute neuro-Behçet’s disease
Interpretation of CRP elevation as an indirect marker of cytokine-driven inflammation
Alternative explanations and limits of causal inference in a single case report
Why simultaneous diagnosis of systemic Behçet’s disease and neuro-Behçet’s disease is diagnostically challenging
Teaching value of MRI-negative neuroinflammatory disease and aseptic meningitis patterns
Clinical importance of recognising hiccups and rhabdomyolysis as potential consequences of severe hyponatraemia
Practical diagnostic pearl: in patients with Behçet-type mucocutaneous lesions plus headache or fever and hyponatraemia, consider acute neuro-Behçet’s disease with SIADH
Practical therapeutic lesson: colchicine may be a reasonable option in selected early cases, but evidence remains limited and standard therapy should still be understood
